title: Primitive Dirichlet L Functions and Functional Equations

items.title: A Dirichlet character modulo q induced by a character modulo a divisor d of q
items.strategy: Fix d | q. Define induction by agreement on integers coprime to q and value zero otherwise; state separately that this is more restrictive than merely composing unit-group characters, since primes dividing q/d create the zero values.

items.title: Primitive Dirichlet characters and the conductor as their least inducing modulus
items.strategy: Define primitive relative to the preceding induction convention and define the conductor only after the unique primitive ancestor theorem below has supplied existence and uniqueness. Record the q = 1 principal character convention explicitly.

items.title: Every Dirichlet character is induced by a unique primitive character of conductor dividing its modulus
items.strategy: Work prime-power by prime-power: identify the least exponent at which the local unit character factors, then use CRT to assemble the local primitive factors. Prove both the induced zero-value condition and uniqueness, not only the unit-group factorisation.

items.title: The L-function of an induced character differs from its primitive ancestor by the omitted finite Euler factors for Re(s) > 1
items.strategy: Compare the absolutely convergent Euler products of chi modulo q and its primitive ancestor chi-star modulo d. State the product over primes dividing q but not d with the correct chi-star(p) factors and keep the half-plane Re(s) > 1 in the claim.

items.title: The Gauss sum tau(chi) with e(x) = exp(2 pi i x)
items.strategy: Define tau(chi) = sum modulo q chi(a)e(a/q), with the modulus and additive-character normalization displayed; this fixes the phase used later in the root number.

items.title: For primitive chi modulo q, the additive twist sum equals conjugate(chi)(m) tau(chi)
items.strategy: For (m,q)=1 change variables by m inverse modulo q. For (m,q)>1, use primitivity to choose a unit congruent to one modulo q/(m,q) on which chi is nontrivial and compare the sum after multiplication; retain the vanishing case rather than silently dividing by m.

items.title: A primitive Dirichlet character chi modulo q satisfies |tau(chi)| squared = q
items.strategy: Sum the twist identity over m modulo q and use character orthogonality to obtain tau(chi) conjugate(tau(chi)) = q. State that the theorem applies only to primitive characters, which is needed for the root-number modulus.

items.title: Parity a of a Dirichlet character, defined by chi(-1) = (-1)^a
items.strategy: Define a in {0,1} and call the two cases even and odd. Explain that q = 1 is even under this convention.

items.title: Fourier transform of a Gaussian for hat f(xi) = integral f(x)e(-x xi) dx
items.strategy: Under e(x) = exp(2 pi i x), prove that the transform of exp(-pi t x squared) is t^(-1/2) exp(-pi xi squared/t) for t > 0, first at t = 1 and then by scaling. State the integrability and normalization hypotheses used by Poisson summation.

items.title: Poisson summation from Fourier invariance of the integer Dirac comb
items.strategy: Prove, for Schwartz functions under the fixed Fourier convention, sum over n f(n) = sum over m hat f(m), by pairing the Fourier-invariant Dirac comb with f. State the extension used for the scaled Gaussian separately so no distributional convention is hidden.

items.title: Twisted Poisson summation for a primitive Dirichlet character
items.strategy: Decompose the integer sum into residue classes modulo q, apply Poisson summation to each translate, and use the primitive Gauss-sum twist. With f_y(x)=exp(-pi x squared y/q), retain the q, y and conjugate-character factors exactly.

items.title: The completed primitive Dirichlet L-function Lambda(s, chi)
items.strategy: For primitive chi modulo q and parity a, define Lambda(s,chi) = (q/pi)^((s+a)/2) Gamma((s+a)/2)L(s,chi). Keep this normalization distinct from the entire xi-function used inside the proof.

items.title: Analytic continuation of Lambda(s, chi) for primitive characters, with the q = 1 zeta exception
items.strategy: Use the even and odd theta-kernel Mellin integrals, their transformed tails from twisted Poisson summation, and the Gaussian transform to continue the completed function. Treat principal primitive chi modulo 1 as the zeta case: Lambda is meromorphic with its familiar poles; otherwise it is entire.

items.title: Functional equation Lambda(s, chi) = epsilon(chi) Lambda(1-s, conjugate chi) for primitive characters
items.strategy: Derive the even and odd theta transformations separately, then unify them with a in {0,1} and epsilon(chi)=(-i)^a tau(chi)/sqrt(q). Check the conjugate-character and i-power against the fixed e(x) convention.

items.title: The primitive Dirichlet root number epsilon(chi) has modulus one
items.strategy: Insert the fixed root-number formula into the Gauss-sum norm identity; the parity factor (-i)^a has modulus one.

items.title: Parity-forced trivial zeros of a primitive nonprincipal Dirichlet L-function, including the s = 0 qualification
items.strategy: Use the gamma poles in the completed-function identity and the entireness result to obtain zeros at negative integers of parity a. Isolate s = 0: for even characters the gamma pole is cancelled only when the completed function is regular there, so the principal q = 1 exception is not asserted as a trivial zero.

title: Primitive Dirichlet L Functions and Functional Equations — Examples

items.title: Primitive ancestors and conductors of small Dirichlet characters
items.strategy: Compute representative characters modulo 4, 8, and 12 by their local components, identify their primitive ancestors, and verify the induced zero-value convention directly.

items.title: Finite Euler factors for a character induced from modulus 4 to modulus 12
items.strategy: Take the primitive quadratic character modulo 4, form its induction modulo 12, write both Euler products in Re(s)>1, and calculate the missing prime-3 factor explicitly.

items.title: The Gauss sum of the primitive odd character modulo 4
items.strategy: Evaluate tau(chi_4)=2i from its two nonzero residues, verify its squared modulus is 4, and identify the resulting root-number phase under the page convention.

items.title: Even and odd theta kernels for the principal character modulo 1 and chi_4
items.strategy: Write the two Mellin kernels with the correct x^a factor, apply the transformed Gaussian, and compare the sign and i-power in the two functional equations.

items.title: The negative odd trivial zeros of the beta function L(s, chi_4)
items.strategy: Use that chi_4 is odd to list the forced zeros at negative odd integers and contrast this with the non-assertion at s=0.

items.title: The character modulo 12 induced by chi_4 has conductor 4, not 12
items.strategy: Compare its values on units and its zeros at nonunits with the induction definition, then invoke uniqueness of the primitive ancestor to rule out conductor 12.

items.title: Changing e(x) to exp(-2 pi i x) conjugates the displayed Gauss-sum phase
items.strategy: Recalculate tau(chi_4) under the opposite additive-character convention and show it is -2i rather than 2i; the norm survives but the root-number formula's phase changes.

title: Number Fields Rings of Integers and Discriminants

items.title: A number field as a finite extension of the rational field
items.strategy: Define a number field K/Q and state n=[K:Q]. This page works in characteristic zero, hence finite extensions are separable when embeddings are introduced.

items.title: The ring of integers O_K as the integral closure of Z in a number field
items.strategy: Define O_K using integrality over Z and identify it with the integral closure inside K. Do not conflate this ring with an arbitrary order.

items.title: An element of a number field is integral over Z exactly when its monic minimal polynomial lies in Z[x]
items.strategy: Apply the integral-element/minimal-polynomial criterion in Q(alpha), using Gauss's lemma to pass between rational and integral coefficients. State both directions and the monicity condition.

items.title: Every element of a number field becomes an algebraic integer after multiplication by a nonzero integer
items.strategy: Start from the rational coefficients of a monic polynomial for alpha, clear denominators by a power-compatible integer N, and exhibit a monic polynomial for N alpha with integer coefficients.

items.title: The trace and norm of an algebraic integer are integers
items.strategy: Use the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by alpha, or equivalently the integral minimal polynomial with its conjugates, to show its coefficients lie in Z; identify the signed constant coefficient and next coefficient with norm and trace.

items.title: An order in a number field as a full-rank Z-subring of O_K
items.strategy: Define an order as a subring containing 1 whose additive group is a full-rank Z-lattice in O_K; record O_K itself as the maximal order and keep full rank part of the definition.

items.title: Integral bases and power integral bases of an order
items.strategy: Define an integral basis as an ordered Z-basis of an order and a power integral basis as 1, alpha, ..., alpha^(n-1). Say that the latter is extra structure and is not assumed for a number field.

items.title: O_K is a free Z-module of rank [K:Q]
items.strategy: Use finite generation of the integral closure over Z, its torsion-free embedding in K, and the PID submodule theorem to obtain freeness. Tensor with Q to identify the rank with [K:Q], without choosing a permanent basis.

items.title: Every order has an integral basis and finite index in O_K
items.strategy: Use the full-rank definition to show O_K/order is a finite torsion abelian group, then apply the PID simultaneous-basis theorem to obtain a Z-basis. Include the converse lattice argument only as needed for the index claim.

items.title: Real and complex embeddings and the signature (r_1,r_2) of a number field
items.strategy: Define r_1 as the number of real embeddings and r_2 as the number of conjugate pairs of nonreal embeddings, so n=r_1+2r_2. State that the embedding determinant first uses all n embeddings, while later signature notation chooses one from each complex pair.

items.title: Discriminant of an ordered Q-basis, an order, and a number field
items.strategy: Define disc(alpha_1,...,alpha_n)=det(Tr(alpha_i alpha_j)) for an ordered Q-basis first. Define disc(A) for an order through an integral basis only after the change-of-basis result, and define disc(K)=disc(O_K) afterwards.

items.title: Discriminants transform by the square of the change-of-basis determinant
items.strategy: Write the trace Gram matrix in the new ordered basis as C transpose G C and take determinants. For a unimodular integral change of basis this proves basis independence of an order discriminant.

items.title: The basis discriminant equals the square of the determinant of the full embedding matrix
items.strategy: For all n embeddings sigma_i:K to C, factor the trace Gram matrix as A transpose A with A=(sigma_i(alpha_j)); use the separable trace formula. Do not replace the full list by one representative of each complex pair in this formula.

items.title: The discriminant of a number field is a well-defined nonzero integer
items.strategy: Use an integral basis and unimodular change of basis for well-definedness, then use distinct embeddings and the embedding determinant for nonvanishing. Integrality follows from integral trace values.

items.title: The discriminant of the power basis equals the discriminant of the minimal polynomial
items.strategy: For alpha of degree n, compare the Vandermonde determinant of its n conjugates with the polynomial discriminant, including the conventional sign. State this for the Q-basis 1,alpha,...,alpha^(n-1), whether or not it is an integral basis.

items.title: For an order A, disc(A) = [O_K:A] squared disc(K)
items.strategy: Choose simultaneous Z-bases of A and O_K; the change matrix has determinant equal in absolute value to the index. Apply the discriminant change-of-basis lemma and retain the square.

items.title: A power order with squarefree discriminant is the full ring of integers
items.strategy: If Z[alpha] is an order and its power-basis discriminant is squarefree, the index-discriminant formula forces [O_K:Z[alpha]]=1. State the necessary hypothesis alpha integral and [Q(alpha):Q]=n.

items.title: The ring of integers of Q(sqrt d) for squarefree d not equal to 1
items.strategy: For squarefree d != 1, prove O_K=Z[(1+sqrt d)/2] when d is 1 modulo 4 and O_K=Z[sqrt d] otherwise. Use the minimal-polynomial criterion plus trace/norm integrality to exclude all other half-integral coefficients.

items.title: The discriminant of Q(sqrt d) for squarefree d not equal to 1
items.strategy: Compute the trace Gram determinant in the integral basis from the quadratic-integers theorem: disc(K)=d for d=1 modulo 4 and 4d otherwise.

items.title: The ring of integers of a number field is a Dedekind domain
items.strategy: Apply the established theorem that the integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite separable extension is Dedekind, with Z and K/Q; match the page's definition of O_K exactly.

title: Number Fields Rings of Integers and Discriminants — Examples

items.title: The ring of integers and discriminant of Q
items.strategy: Verify O_Q=Z from the rational-root/minimal-polynomial criterion, use basis (1), and compute discriminant 1.

items.title: Integral bases and discriminants of the Gaussian and Eisenstein integers
items.strategy: Apply the quadratic formula to d=-1 and d=-3, displaying bases (1,i) and (1,(1+sqrt(-3))/2) and their discriminants -4 and -3.

items.title: The integral basis and discriminant of Q(sqrt 5)
items.strategy: Show O_K=Z[(1+sqrt 5)/2], compute discriminant 5, and contrast it with the discriminant 20 of the nonmaximal power order Z[sqrt 5].

items.title: A pure cubic field whose displayed power order is certified maximal by a squarefree discriminant
items.strategy: Use a source-supported pure cubic polynomial with squarefree polynomial discriminant, verify its root is integral and has the stated degree, then apply the squarefree power-basis criterion. Include the arithmetic discriminant computation rather than asserting monogeneity.

items.title: The nonmaximal quadratic order Z[sqrt 5] inside O_Q(sqrt 5)
items.strategy: Write both integral bases, compute index 2, and verify the order-index discriminant formula 20=2 squared times 5.

items.title: Index 2 explains why factorisation modulo 2 in Z[sqrt 5] is not a factorisation statement for O_Q(sqrt 5)
items.strategy: Use the nonmaximal order inclusion to exhibit the missing half-integral element and explain, with a concrete polynomial reduction, which inference from a power order is invalid before maximality is established.

items.title: A fully proved nonmonogenic number-field example remains a sourced authoring obligation
items.strategy: Do not assert a particular counterexample here. The design reserves the B-page slot for a concrete nonmonogenic field, but the opened primary source only gives an unsupported general warning in its later discussion; authoring requires a fetched source that proves a named example and supplies enough detail to verify nonmonogeneity.
